2017_105_032117mtg.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of March 21, 2017 at the Services Building — the meeting where the Early Childhood Center becomes a plan. Item 8.F authorizes marketing three parcels of surplus vacant land, directs that the proceeds be restricted in the Capital Maintenance Fund toward the Early Childhood Center, appoints TMP Architecture as architect of record at a fee not to exceed $933,716 for phases 1 through 4, and settles the shape of the Section 1 property — frontage split off for sale, the remainder preserved in perpetuity. The meeting also adopts Budget Amendment #2, awards Bid Pack 19 at $443,960.00 and Bid Pack 20 at $1,044,052.90, and buys $80,000.00 of interior painting and $28,246.00 of pool lockers.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, March 21, 2017, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
The Mission Moment honors Troy College & Career dual enrollment students. The program has grown from **eight students who started at Baker Community College over nine years ago while attending Niles Community High School** to **44 students today** — nine of them from Intersect — taking between one and four classes at Oakland and Macomb Community Colleges and Oakland University. **Nearly thirty percent of Troy College & Career students are currently enrolled in college.** Six are recognized, spanning the range from Amanda DiGiovanni, with 21 credits earned at OCC and in her fourth semester of dual enrollment, to Mohammad Abulaban, who just started his first class. Each completed a College Prep course and is enrolled in a College Seminar covering time management, essay writing, study and test-taking, educational career planning and scholarship applications.

The second item recognizes **Kristin Piotrowski** for Reading Recovery Teacher Leader certification, a role requiring an academic year of full-time professional development at a registered university training center.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the February 7 special meeting, closed session and workshop, the February 28 meeting, and the January 2017 Treasurer's Report.

**Treasurer's Report — January 2017**
Total check disbursements are $5,621,657.71, the General Fund group $4,614,209.13 and the General Fund (101) itself $4,235,073.21. Adding $2,823,482.13 of wire transfers, $110,145.11 of P-Card purchases and $40,086.89 of ACH debits, less **$270,259.19 of prior period voids** — an unusually large reversal — total disbursements in period are $8,325,112.65.

**Business 8.A — Budget Amendment #2**
The 2016-17 amendment covers the General Fund (Amendment 2) plus first amendments to Food Service, Troy Career Center, Adult Education and Community Service, Capital Projects and Capital Maintenance. Amended appropriations: **General Fund $145,342,591**, Capital Projects $13,123,639, Food Service $3,903,967, Adult Education and Community Service $3,389,445, Capital Maintenance $2,469,355 and Troy Career Center $1,865,754.

General Fund revenue rises $707,243 to $145,655,496 — state up $348,158 to $96,756,588, federal up $335,602 to $3,757,332, incoming transfers up $204,812 to $8,158,473, **local down $181,329 to $36,983,103** — against an unchanged July 1 fund balance of $21,532,285, for $167,187,781 available to appropriate. Instruction rises $231,073 to $99,492,517 and support services $294,500 to $45,710,937, the increases spread thinly across every line rather than concentrated.

Two other funds move sharply. Adult Education and Community Service expenditures rise $431,844 to $3,389,445, driven by a **$317,371 increase in salaries**, cutting the projected June 30 balance from $633,846 to $242,917. The Capital Projects Funds show $40,000,000 of bond proceeds unchanged, with site improvements up $1,366,121 to $1,616,121 and equipment up $1,158,508 to $1,708,508, offset by bond expenditures down $600,000. The Troy Career Center's budget falls $237,467 to $1,865,754.

**Business 8.B–8.E — construction and maintenance**

| Item | Award | Fund |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bid Pack 20 — site work | $1,044,052.90 | 2016 Capital Projects |
| Bid Pack 19 — Larson/IAE/doors | $443,960.00 | 2016 Capital Projects |
| Interior painting | General Painting Company LLC — $80,000.00 | Capital Maintenance |
| Troy High pool lockers | Brainard Enterprises Inc. — $28,246.00 | Capital Maintenance |

Bid Pack 19 renovates the old office area at Larson into a collaborative teaching and learning space, creates a storage area in the old pool shower area at IA East, and replaces interior and exterior doors at Barnard, Bemis, Wass, Larson, Athens, Troy High and the Administration Building: M.L. Schoenherr general trades $281,600.00, Contrast Mechanical $54,000.00, Great Lakes Power electrical $68,000.00 and $40,360.00 of contingency.

Bid Pack 20 covers site work at Troy High, Boulan Park, Bemis, Hamilton, Hill and the Administration and Services Buildings: Nagle Paving sitework with alternates 3, 4, 5 and 7 at $846,920.00, J. Ranck electrical with alternate E2 at $102,219.00, and $94,913.90 of contingency. The alternates selected in post-bid analysis are additional parking, signage and striping at Bemis ($79,000.00), mill and crack repair in lieu of seal coat at the Services Building ($58,375.00) and the Administration Building ($35,200.00), and Hill site work ($39,760.00).

**Business 8.F — the Early Childhood Center takes shape**
The district has been conducting pre-sale investigations of district-owned vacant property. The resolution recites that the Board values the real property it owns, that it desires to develop an Early Childhood Center to serve the preschool programs, and that it wishes to **consider the sale of certain surplus vacant real property in order to offset long term debt for that development** — authorizing administration, Clark Hill PLC and real estate consultant Great Northern Consulting Group to explore, market and analyze those sales, with any offer or agreement to come back to the Board for approval.

Six operative clauses:

1. Investigate **preserving the Section 1 property**, except the Square Lake frontage, which will be split into its own parcel and marketed; the remainder may be preserved in perpetuity by the district or through a conservation easement or similar agreement.
2. Authorize marketing **Section 11** for sale.
3. Develop the Early Childhood Center on **approximately 8 acres of Section 16**, preserving the balance.
4. Appoint **TMP Architecture** as architect of record to commence design per its March 10, 2017 proposal, at a cost **not to exceed $933,716** for phases 1 through 4, from the Capital Maintenance Fund.
5. Costs of selling property are an approved Capital Maintenance Fund professional services expenditure.
6. **Revenue from the property sales shall be restricted in the Capital Maintenance Fund for use toward developing the Early Childhood Center.**

TMP's proposal quotes a total architectural and engineering fee of **$1,167,144.00, based on 6% of an estimated construction cost of $19,452,406** — covering architectural, furniture, mechanical, electrical, civil and landscaping design but not technology consulting. By phase: schematic design 15% / $175,072; design development 20% / $233,429; construction documents 40% / $466,858; bidding 5% / $58,357; construction 18% / $210,066; close out 2% / $23,343. The Board authorizes only the first four phases here.

This single resolution is the origin of nearly everything the district would do with land over the following two years — the Section 1 split and conservation easement, the Section 16 sale, and the preschool that would be financed by bond issue in 2018.

Agenda packet for the regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, March 21, 2017, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Recognition — A. TSD Mission Moment: Troy College & Career Dual Enrollment Students, B. Kris Piotrowski, Reading Recovery/Teacher Leader Certification; 3. Additions & Deletions; 4. Public Communication (agenda items); 5. General – Consent Agenda — A. Minutes of the February 7, 2017 Board of Education Special Meeting, B. Minutes of the February 7, 2017 Board of Education Closed Session, C. Minutes of the February 7, 2017 Board of Education Workshop, D. Minutes of the February 28, 2017 Board of Education Meeting, E. Treasurer's Report – January 2017; 6. Personnel; 7. Curriculum; 8. Business — A. Consideration: Budget Amendment #2, B. Consideration: Bid Pack 19 – IAE Pool Storage, Larson Old Office Renovation & Door Replacement, C. Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

**Recognition 2.A: Troy College & Career dual enrollment students.** The Board honors a group of high school students enrolled in college classes while completing their high school course requirements. The item traces the program's growth: it began with eight students who, over nine years earlier, started classes at Baker Community College while attending Niles Community High School. Currently 44 students, including nine from Intersect, are enrolled in between one and four classes at Oakland and Macomb Community Colleges and even Oakland University while completing high school requirements. Nearly thirty percent of Troy College & Career students, both in and outside the Troy School District, are currently enrolled in college.

The six students recognized are described as exemplifying the spectrum of learners the school serves, from one finishing her second year at OCC to the newest student taking his first college course, and as representing many who choose to attend TCC specifically for its dual enrollment opportunities. They are Mohammad Abulaban, who just started his first semester with one class at OCC; Amanda DiGiovanni, who has earned 21 credits at OCC and is taking three classes in her second full year, her fourth semester of dual enrollment; Amber (Parker) Gilchrist, who has earned three credits and is taking one class for the winter semester; Erin Long, who has earned 10 credits at OCC and is taking three classes in the vet tech program at MCC in her second semester; Nathan Murduff, who has earned 9 credits and is taking three classes in his second semester at OCC; and Carolyn Schaeper, who has earned 3 credits at OCC and is taking four classes in her second semester.

All six completed a College Prep course to ready them for post-secondary education and are now enrolled in a College Seminar class providing personal assistance with time management and class organization, content areas, essay writing, study and test-taking, educational career planning, learning how to apply for scholarships, and monitoring of grades, with collaboration among peers creating what the item calls a totally supportive environment for academic achievement.

**Recognition 2.B: Reading Recovery Teacher Leader certification.** The Board recognizes Kristin Piotrowski. The item explains the credential: a teacher leader candidate attends a registered university training center in the United States, or a regional institute in Canada, for an academic year of full-time professional development. The complex role requires them to become Reading Recovery teachers; to develop an academic understanding of the theoretical concepts on which Reading Recovery is based and the flexibility to consider new concepts and practices; to test practice against theoretical concepts; and to critically appraise Reading Recovery's strengths and problem spots as well as competing explanations for its success.

**Consent agenda.** Minutes of the February 7, 2017 special meeting, closed session and workshop; minutes of the February 28, 2017 regular meeting; and the January 2017 Treasurer's Report.

**Treasurer's Report, January 2017.** General Fund (101) check disbursements are $4,235,073.21, with Total General Fund of $4,614,209.13 and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS of $5,621,657.71. Adding ACH debits of $40,086.89, outgoing wire transfers of $2,823,482.13 and P-Card purchases of $110,145.11, and subtracting prior period void disbursements of $270,259.19, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $8,325,112.65. The void figure is large — most months in these packets run from nothing to a few tens of thousands — indicating a substantial reversal of previously issued checks in the period. The middle sections of the packet are the January check register run by fund.

**Business 8.A: the 2016-17 Budget Amendment Resolution.** The amendment covers the General Fund (Amendment 2), the Food Service Fund (Amendment 1), the Troy Career Center (Amendment 1), the Adult Education and Community Service Fund (Amendment 1), the Capital Projects Funds (Amendment 1) and the Capital Maintenance Fund (Amendment 1). The item notes the resolution need not be read in its entirety but must be made part of the official minutes, and the resolution amends and approves the general appropriations and budget for fiscal year 2016-17 for those funds as attached and made part of the official minutes of the March 21, 2017 regular meeting.

The amended fund totals are: General Fund $145,342,591; Food Service Fund $3,903,967; Troy Career Center Fund $1,865,754; Adult Education and Community Service Fund $3,389,445; Capital Projects Fund $13,123,639; and Capital Maintenance Fund $2,469,355.

On General Fund revenue, comparing the proposed amended budget to the amended budget: state revenue rises $348,158 to $96,756,588; federal revenue rises $335,602 to $3,757,332; incoming transfers and other rise $204,812 to $8,158,473; and local revenue falls $181,329 to $36,983,103. Total revenues and incoming transfers rise $707,243 to $145,655,496. Fund balance at July 1 is unchanged at $21,532,285, so total available to appropriate rises $707,243 to $167,187,781.

On General Fund expenditures, basic programs rise $26,142 to $81,760,617 and total instruction rises $231,073 to $99,492,517. In support services: pupil rises $29,473 to $10,490,258; instructional staff rises $80,413 to $7,655,515; general administration rises $16,533 to $2,301,063; school administration rises $6,027 to $7,297,872; business services rises $5,200 to $1,140,685; operations and maintenance rises $71,187 to $9,179,819; pupil transportation rises $22,720 to $3,412,537; central services rises $37,834 to $2,525,281; and athletics and other support services rise $25,113 to $1,707,907, for total support services of $45,710,937, up $294,500. Unlike the following year's amendment, which swung general administration by more than $1.3 million, this one moves every line modestly in the same direction.

The Food Service Fund amendment appropriates $3,903,967, with state revenue down $12,219 to $101,268, federal revenue up $38,494 to $900,000, and a new $100,000 repairs and rentals line where the original budget had none; supplies and materials hold at $1,448,795.

The Troy Career Center Fund tells a harder story: total revenues fall $237,467 to $1,865,754, with $18,730 of new local sources partly offsetting, and expenditures fall by the same $237,467, salaries dropping $67,184 to $844,510. The fund's balance falls from $1,631,810 to $1,610,824 at July 1 and its projected June 30 balance from $1,320,870 to $1,144,421, a reduction of $176,450.

The Adult Education and Community Service Fund appropriates $3,389,445. Local revenue rises $12,190 to $3,476,835 and the July 1 fund balance is restated upward $28,725 to $155,527, for $3,632,362 available to appropriate, up $40,915. But expenditures rise $431,844 to $3,389,445 — salaries alone up $317,371 to $1,007,453, employee benefits up $94,656 to $446,014, purchased services up $17,245 to $1,111,029, supplies and materials up $2,072 to $156,851 and capital outlay up $500 to $2,000, with repairs and rentals holding at $9,581, other expenditures at $6,517 and outgoing transfers at $650,000. Excess revenues over expenditures accordingly fall from $507,044 to $87,390, and the projected June 30 balance from $633,846 to $242,917 — a $390,929 reduction, the sharpest single movement in the amendment.

The Capital Projects Funds appropriate $13,123,639. Bond proceeds hold at $40,000,000 and earnings on investments rise $25,000 to $125,000. On the expenditure side, site improvements rise $1,366,121 to $1,616,121 and equipment rises $1,158,508 to $1,708,508, while building permits fall $25,000 to nothing and bond expenditures fall $600,000 to $145,000, with no school bus line. The site improvement and equipment increases are the budget catching up with the bid packs the Board is approving in the same meeting.

**Business 8.B: Bond Construction Bid Pack 19.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on the Larson office renovation, the IA East storage room and interior and exterior door replacements at multiple district buildings, reviewed by TMP Associates, Peter Basso & Associates and Barton Malow.

Rob Carson's March 15, 2017 memorandum on RFP 9834 records that the RFP was issued February 15, 2017; that the scope is to renovate the old office area at Larson into a collaborative teaching and learning space, create a storage area in the old pool shower area at IAE, and remove and replace interior and exterior doors at Barnard, Bemis and Wass Elementary Schools, Larson Middle School, Athens and Troy High Schools and the Administration Building; and that the RFP specified 3 bid categories opened on March 1, 2017. He recommends, on low bid per category: category 060000 general trades, M.L. Schoenherr Construction, $281,600.00; category 230000 mechanical, Contrast Mechanical, $54,000.00; category 260000 electrical, Great Lakes Power & Lighting, $68,000.00; plus contingency of $40,360.00, for a total of $443,960.00. All proposals were reviewed and qualified by the bond team of TMP Associates, Peter Basso & Associates, Michelle Kerns and Barton Malow, with a separate purchase order to be issued for each bid category. The resolution awards Bid Pack 19 with $443,960.00 approved as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

The IA East storage room being created in the old pool shower area is worth noting: the pool at International Academy East is already closed in March 2017, and the district would convert the pool area itself into classrooms under Bid Pack 23 at the end of 2018.

**Business 8.C: Bond Construction Bid Pack 20, site work.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on site work at various district buildings — Carson's February 28, 2017 memorandum heads it Bid Package 20, bond construction and site work at Troy High, Boulan Park, Bemis, Hamilton, Hill and the Administration and Services Buildings — reviewed by TMP Associates, Peter Basso & Associates and Barton Malow.

The RFP specified 2 bid categories. Carson recommends, on low bid per category with a contingency budget: category 320000 sitework, Nagle Paving with alternates 3, 4, 5 and 7, $846,920.00; category 260000 electrical, J. Ranck with alternate E2, $102,219.00; and a contingency budget of $94,913.90, for a total budget recommendation of $1,044,052.90. All proposals were reviewed and qualified by the bond team of TMP Associates, PEA Civil Engineering and Barton Malow, and the funding is from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. The resolution awards bid pack 20 on those terms.

The bid summary shows base bid prices across eight bidders — GLPL $156,000.00, J. Ranck $89,442.00, McNulty $95,000.00, Metro $157,000.00, Shoreview $138,000.00 on the electrical side, and ASI $660,000.00, Cortis $636,600.00, Nagle $634,585.00 on the sitework side — with per-building breakdowns for Troy High, Bemis, Boulan, Hamilton, Hill, Services and Admin. The alternates priced are: No. 1, Troy High concrete in lieu of asphalt; No. 2, Troy High ramp in lieu of concrete; No. E2, Bemis site electrical; No. 3, Bemis additional parking, signage and striping; No. 4, Services Building mill and crack repair in lieu of seal coat; No. 5, Administration Building mill and crack repair in lieu of seal coat; No. 6, Hamilton; and No. 7, Hill. The ones actually selected in post-bid analysis are Bemis additional parking, signage and striping at $79,000.00, Services mill and crack repair at $58,375.00, Administration mill and crack repair at $35,200.00, and Hill at $39,760.00 — with the apparent low bidder total shown as $948,639.00 across the selected scope.

**Business 8.D: pool locker replacement, Troy High.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on the pool locker replacement project at Troy High School, reviewed by Rob Carson. The resolution awards the work to Brainard Enterprises Inc. in the amount of $28,246.00 as an expenditure of the capital maintenance fund.

**Business 8.E: interior painting.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on interior painting at various district buildings, reviewed by Rob Carson, whose March 1, 2017 memorandum covers RFP 9837, contracted painting recommendation. The resolution awards the interior painting to General Painting Company LLC in the amount of $80,000.00 as an expenditure of the capital maintenance fund.

**Business 8.F: district-owned property.** This is the meeting's substantive act. The district has been conducting pre-sale investigations of district-owned vacant property and offers the resolution for consideration.

The recitals: the Board's mission is to ensure learning for all members of the school community; the Board appreciates and values the real property owned by the district; the district desires to develop an Early Childhood Center to service its preschool programs; the Board desires to explore and consider the sale of certain surplus, vacant real property in order to offset long term debt for the development of an Early Childhood Center; and the Board desires to authorize the district's administration, its legal counsel Clark Hill PLC, and its real estate consultant Great Northern Consulting Group to explore, market and analyze the sale of certain surplus vacant real property as outlined below, with the understanding that any offers or agreements will be brought before the Board for approval.

The six resolved clauses:

1. The district authorizes administration to further investigate the preservation of the Section 1 property, with the exception of the frontage on Square Lake, which will be split into its own parcel and marketed for sale. The remainder of the land may be preserved in perpetuity either by the district or through a conservation easement or other similar form of agreement.
2. The district authorizes the marketing of Section 11 property for purposes of sale.
3. The district desires to develop an Early Childhood Center on approximately 8 acres of Section 16 and preserve the balance of the subject property.
4. The district appoints TMP Architecture as the architect of record and authorizes TMP Architecture to commence the design process for an Early Childhood Center in accordance with their submitted proposal for services dated March 10, 2017. The cost of services is not to exceed $933,716 to complete phases 1 through 4 of the proposal and is approved as an expenditure of the Capital Maintenance Fund.
5. The cost associated with the selling of property is an approved expenditure of the Capital Maintenance Fund Professional Services Budget.
6. Revenue generated from these property sales shall be restricted in the Capital Maintenance Fund for the purposes of using toward the development of the Early Childhood Center.

John Waldrop, AIA, principal and project manager at TMP Architecture, Inc. of Bloomfield Hills, writes to Rick West on March 10, 2017 with the proposal. He thanks West for the opportunity and notes it has been a pleasure to work with him to develop the project scope and initial concepts, and includes a breakdown of proposed fees by phase based on their previous agreement for the 2013 TSD Bond projects. The fee for architectural and engineering services is $1,167,144.00, based on 6% of an estimated construction cost of $19,452,406, and includes architectural, furniture, mechanical, electrical, civil and landscaping design services but not technology consulting services or design.

The fee by phase is: 1, schematic design, 15%, $175,072; 2, design development, 20%, $233,429; 3, construction documents, 40%, $466,858; 4, bidding, 5%, $58,357; 5, construction, 18%, $210,066; and 6, close out, 2%, $23,343 — totalling $1,167,144. The Board's authorization covers phases 1 through 4 only, at not to exceed $933,716, holding back the construction and close-out phases until the project is actually built.

This resolution is the origin point for most of what the district would do with land and buildings over the next two years, and it is worth reading against what actually followed. The Section 1 disposition described here in a single sentence — frontage split off and marketed, remainder preserved in perpetuity or by conservation easement — is exactly the structure the Board would adopt in three separate resolutions in March 2018, over two dissenting votes and after months of public comment. The Section 16 land is here designated as the Early Childhood Center site on approximately 8 acres, with the balance preserved; in the event, the entire 19.43-acre Section 16 parcel was sold to Mondrian Properties in March 2018 and the preschool was built at 205 Square Lake Road instead. And the financing premise stated here — selling surplus land to offset long term debt, with proceeds restricted toward the center — is the plan that the December 2017 construction resolution and the 2018 bond issue would ultimately supersede.

The estimated construction cost TMP works from, $19,452,406, is also close to what the project ultimately cost when bid 9855 was awarded in March 2018.

Read as a whole, the March 2017 packet is a district converting real estate into a building. Item 8.F sets the whole chain in motion — the consultants, the architect, the parcels, and the rule that the money must stay restricted to the preschool — while the four construction items around it, totalling roughly a million and a half dollars of site work, doors, painting and lockers, are the ordinary maintenance of the buildings it already has.
